processing: Handled as raw pu-erh normally is: pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then sold loose or pressed, with no ripening pile.
harvest_season: Not documented in detail; in Yiwu generally, spring is the prized picking.
appearance_dry: As with other Yiwu raw teas, long dark-green large leaves, usually pressed.
appearance_liquor: As with other young Yiwu raw teas, clear golden yellow.
appearance_wet: Supple olive-green large leaves, typical of the class.
taste_profile: Said to be close in quality to neighbouring Yishanmo, which is known for high aroma and a soft liquor; detailed notes for Xiangchunlin itself are scarce.

brewing.notes: Treat it like other Yiwu raw tea: boiling or near-boiling water and short early steeps, using a small vessel if you have only a little.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year as raw pu-erh usually is, in very small quantities since output is tiny. Spring lots are the ones to look for, and no long record of aged vintages under this name is documented.
description:
Xiangchunlin, Toon Tree Forest, is a small garden area of the Han section of Dingjiazhai in Yiwu. Far less known than its neighbour Yishanmo, it is grouped with it as one of the larger areas of cultivated old tea trees in the Six Great Tea Mountains.

Nothing about its processing is recorded as unusual, so expect the standard raw pu-erh steps of pan-firing, rolling and sun-drying.

Its quality is said to be close to Yishanmo's, with the aroma and soft liquor associated with Yiwu. Brew it the way you would other Yiwu teas, and pay attention to how the sweetness develops.

Output is very small and few drinkers know the name, so a large or cheap supply should raise questions. Trying it alongside a Yishanmo is the natural comparison.
history: Little is documented about Xiangchunlin. It is known as part of the Dingjiazhai gardens of Yiwu, but when the trees were planted and who first sold the tea under this name are not recorded.
